summary: This RFC specifies a Telnet option for exchanging terminal type information. It supersedes RFC 884, with the one change that the TERMINAL-TYPE IS sub-negotiation is sent only in answer to a SEND request. It was replaced by RFC 1091.

plainLanguage.summary: When you connect, your computer can say what kind of screen it has when asked. This version only answers after being asked.

questions: how does telnet negotiate terminal type
what is the telnet terminal-type option
what is option code 24 in telnet
subtitle: Letting Telnet servers learn what kind of screen is on the other end

tldr.problem: Telnet servers need to know what kind of terminal a user has connected so they can send appropriate display commands (colors, cursor movement, etc.), not just plain text.
tldr.mechanism: A new Telnet option (code 24) allows the client and server to negotiate terminal type information. The client tells the server its terminal type (e.g., IBM-3278-2) in response to a request, using a simple ASCII string.
tldr.outcome: This enabled Telnet to drive full-screen terminal applications with special effects beyond the Network Virtual Terminal baseline. RFC 1091 later refined the specification.

today: RFC 930 is standard and has not been obsoleted. However, RFC 1091 provides a refined specification for the same option. The Telnet Terminal Type option remains part of standard Telnet implementations.

sections.title: The Terminal Type Option
sections.content:
RFC 930 defines a new option for the Telnet protocol to allow exchange of terminal type information. Telnet servers use this to determine what kind of terminal is at the other end of the connection and can then customize the data sent to match the terminal's capabilities. Without this option, all hosts assume a generic Network Virtual Terminal and cannot use special features like color, cursor addressing, or other advanced display functions.

This is a minor update to RFC 884, changing only that TERMINAL-TYPE information should be sent only in response to a request, not spontaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet lets the remote computer ask your computer what kind of screen you have, so it can send you the right kind of display commands.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: The option uses Telnet's standard negotiation. First, the parties exchange WILL and DO commands to agree that terminal type exchange is allowed. Once agreed, only the sender of the DO command may request terminal type information using TERMINAL-TYPE SEND (code 1). Only the sender of the WILL command may transmit type information using TERMINAL-TYPE IS (code 0), and only in response to a SEND request. The terminal type itself is an ASCII string, up to 40 characters, such as 'IBM-3278-2' or 'VT100'.
sections.plainLanguage: The computers first agree to talk about terminal type. Then the server asks, and the client answers with its terminal type name.

sections.title: Implementation Guidance
sections.content: The official list of terminal type names is maintained in the Assigned Numbers registry to reduce spelling confusion. If a terminal is known by more than one name (a specific model and a more generic family), the client should respond to successive SEND requests with alternatives, from most to least specific. The client stops when it repeats the same answer twice. Servers should stop requesting after receiving the same answer twice. The special type name 'UNKNOWN' is used when the terminal type cannot be determined. Case is insignificant in terminal type names.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a standard list of terminal names so everyone spells them the same way. If a terminal goes by multiple names, you can offer them one at a time until the server recognizes one.
